chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn Isa from Yunus from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, and Humayd ibn Ziyad from Ibn Sama'a from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I said to him: A man and a woman were buried when a house fell on them and they died. He said: The man inherits from the woman and the woman inherits from the man.

I said: Indeed Abu Hanifa has introduced something regarding them in this matter. He said: What did he introduce? I said: Two brothers, non-Arabs, who have no heir except their mawla (manumitters/freemen). One of them had one hundred thousand dirhams known to him, and the other had nothing. They boarded a ship and drowned, and the one hundred thousand dirhams were taken out. What should be done with it?
He said: It is given to the mawla of the one who had nothing, and the other had none. Then he said: I do not object to what he introduced in it; he is correct, it is thus.

Then he said: The wealth is given to the mawla of the one who had nothing, provided the other did not have wealth that the mawla of the other would inherit. Thus, there is nothing for the mawla of the other.

key_terms.سَقَطَ عَلَيْهِمَا الْبَيْتُ: The house fell upon them (simultaneous death)
key_terms.مَوَالِيهِمَا: Their mawla (plural of mawla, referring to manumitters or patrons)

ai.seo_question: How is inheritance distributed when a husband and wife, or two brothers with a common mawla, die simultaneously?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the principle of mutual inheritance (*tarathuth*) between spouses dying simultaneously, while also addressing the specific legal nuance of *mawla* (patron) inheritance for non-Arab converts. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates Abu Hanifa’s reasoning in a case of two brothers with unequal wealth, ruling that the wealth of the richer brother passes to the mawla of the poorer brother, provided the latter had no other assets to trigger his own mawla's claim. This highlights the Shia emphasis on the continuity of the patron-client relationship in inheritance when direct heirs are absent.
